title: What went right this week: the good news that matters

What went right this week: the good news that matters

The ‘alternative Nobel prize’, global progress on ageism, and a boost for gorillas, plus more

Actual Article Body:
The ‘alternative Nobel prize’, global progress on ageism, and a boost for gorillas, plus more good news

The ‘alternative Nobel prize’, global progress on ageism, and a boost for gorillas, plus more good news

Four individuals and organisations challenging authoritarian rule, patriarchal violence and unchecked AI development have been awarded an ‘alternative Nobel prize’.

Better known as the Right Livelihood Award, the prize champions those offering “resistance to systems that push people to the margins”. All this year’s recipients are women or female-led organisations.

Eritrean computer scientist Timnit Gebru (main image) was one of them. Founder of the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, she was praised “for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence, and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency”.

Lawyer Jalila Haider from Pakistan was another recipient. She was commended for challenging “ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution” in her community, a Persian-speaking ethnic group called Hazara.

The two winning organisations were the Rural Women’s Assembly and the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association. The former empowers women in Africa to defend land, seed and bodily autonomy against corporate dispossession. The latter works to safeguard Georgian democracy “in the face of an autocratic crackdown”.

Announcing the recipients, Ole von Uexkull, executive director of Right Livelihood, said the winners were “rewriting the rules that autocrats, patriarchs and Silicon Valley’s most powerful men assumed were theirs to write alone”.

Image: Zakithi Sibandze from the Rural Women’s Assembly. Credit: Right Livelihood

Low-lying nations vulnerable to rising seas will continue to exist as sovereign states even if their land disappears, world leaders have agreed for the first time.

In a welcome victory for multinationalism, UN member states unanimously agreed to protect the sovereignty of climate-vulnerable island nations should they be inundated. Despite having aggressively undermined climate science under the Trump presidency, the US did not oppose the declaration.

It means that states would retain control over their old maritime borders, even if their land disappears. Until now, it has been unclear what would happen in such an event.

The UN declaration echoes a recent ruling by the International Court of Justice, which affirmed low-lying nations’ sovereign rights. Only now have world leaders endorsed that ruling.

Surangel Whipps Jr, President of the Republic of Palau, welcomed the declaration. “Sea level rise threatens our coasts, our homes and our ways of life,” he said. “[But] it does not threaten our legal rights or our standing as states.”

Image: Shalamov

More countries than ever before are legislating to guard against ageism, strengthening care for the elderly and creating age-friendly environments.

So finds a new UN report, which found that “real progress” has been made globally to ensure elderly people are healthier, more comfortable and more visible in society.

The report highlights a sharp rise in the number of countries with legislation to help prevent age-based discrimination – up from 44.5% in 2018 to 57.7% today. The number of countries with national long-term care policies has also risen, it said, from 49% in 2023 to 56.7% today.

“More countries are legislating against ageism, providing integrated care, strengthening long-term care systems, and creating age-friendly environments than ever before, in all regions and income levels,” said the World Health Organization’s Dr Ritu Sadana.

However, she warned that “progress is uneven”, and called on nations to step up their commitments to elderly citizens.

Image: Halfpoint

The Norwegian government has unveiled the country’s largest ever marine reserve and promised robust protection of the new site.
